title: A2: Recalibrating the intercept
text:
The straight transfer from HOAL to Raasdorf_2024 failed. For clay, almost all of the error was one constant offset: the HOAL line predicted too high at every Raasdorf sample by about the same amount. A constant offset is something we can correct.
The idea is to keep the HOAL line and slide it up or down to the Raasdorf level, without changing its slope. This is called recalibration of the intercept (also “recalibration-in-the-large” or “bias correction”). It is a standard way to update a model for a new setting (janssen2008?; dardenne2004?).
The page has four steps:

title: A2: Recalibrating the intercept
text:
Site of the study






Figure 1: Site study and sampling points

title: A2: Recalibrating the intercept
text:
Set up

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

from pipeline import load_data
from plot_style import COLORS, LINE_COLOR, add_header

hoal, raasdorf_2024, raasdorf_2026 = load_data()

title: A2: Recalibrating the intercept
text:
Step 1: the straight transfer
We apply the HOAL line for clay and silt, using U238, to the Raasdorf_2024 points. Nothing is refitted.

chosen = {"Clay": "U238", "Silt": "U238"}

hoal_fits = {}
predictions = {}
for target, predictor in chosen.items():
    fit = stats.linregress(hoal[predictor], hoal[target])
    hoal_fits[target] = fit
    predictions[target] = fit.intercept + fit.slope * raasdorf_2024[predictor]

The error of each point is predicted minus observed. We split it into two parts:

bias: the average error, which is how far the predictions are off in one direction.
spread: how much the errors differ from one another around that average.

The RMSE combines the two: RMSE² = bias² + spread².

rows = []
for target in chosen:
    error = predictions[target] - raasdorf_2024[target]
    rows.append({
        "texture": target,
        "bias": error.mean(),
        "spread": error.std(ddof=0),
        "RMSE": np.sqrt((error ** 2).mean()),
    })

pd.DataFrame(rows).round(1)

title: A2: Recalibrating the intercept
text:
Step 2: what the shift does
Every dot below is one Raasdorf sample, placed at its error for clay. Zero means a perfect prediction.
The top panel is the straight transfer. The dots sit far from zero, which is the bias, and they are spread over a width, which is the spread. The bottom panel is the same dots after the intercept shift: every prediction is moved by the same amount, so the whole group slides onto zero.

target = "Clay"
error = predictions[target] - raasdorf_2024[target]
shifted = error - error.mean()

jitter = np.random.default_rng(0).uniform(-0.3, 0.3, len(error))
low = min(error.min(), shifted.min()) - 4
high = max(error.max(), shifted.max()) + 4

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 5.5), sharex=True)
panels = [(error, "Straight HOAL transfer"), (shifted, "After shifting the intercept")]

for ax, (values, title) in zip(axes, panels):
    bias = values.mean()
    bias = 0.0 if abs(bias) < 0.05 else bias
    spread = values.std(ddof=0)
    rmse = np.sqrt((values ** 2).mean())

    # the bullseye: error = 0
    ax.axvline(0, color=LINE_COLOR, linewidth=2)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.97, "perfect (error = 0)", color=LINE_COLOR, fontsize=8, va="bottom")

    ax.scatter(values, jitter, s=55, color=COLORS[target], edgecolor="white", zorder=3)

    # bias: the distance from the bullseye to the centre of the dots
    if abs(bias) > 0.5:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(bias, -0.6), xytext=(0, -0.6),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="#64748B"))
        ax.text(bias / 2, -0.5, "bias", ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#64748B")

    # spread: how wide the dots are around their own centre
    ax.annotate("", xy=(bias + spread, 0.75), xytext=(bias - spread, 0.75),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="#334155"))
    ax.text(bias, 0.82, "spread", ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#334155")

    ax.set_ylim(-1, 1.1)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    add_header(ax, f"{title}   bias = {bias:.1f}   spread = {spread:.1f}   RMSE = {rmse:.1f}")

axes[1].set_xlim(low, high)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Error = predicted − observed (percentage points of clay)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.55)
plt.show()








The shift removes the bias and leaves the spread untouched, so the RMSE falls to the size of the spread, and no lower.






WarningThis improvement is too good to trust



We set the shift using the same samples we are scoring. Moving the line by the average error makes the average error zero by construction, so the bottom panel always looks good. The next step tests it fairly.

title: A2: Recalibrating the intercept
text:
Step 3: the honest test
To test the shift on samples that were not used to set it, we use leave-one-out. For each Raasdorf sample in turn:

Leave that sample out.
Set the shift from the other 18 samples.
Use the shifted line to predict the sample that was left out, and record the error.

After 19 rounds, every sample has been predicted by a shift that never saw it. The table compares five numbers:

RMSE straight transfer: from step 1.
RMSE shifted, same points: the optimistic number from step 2.
RMSE shifted, leave-one-out: the honest error of the recalibrated line.
RMSE local mean, leave-one-out: the error from ignoring HOAL altogether and predicting the average Raasdorf texture. This is the benchmark the recalibrated line has to beat.
slope of observed on predicted: does the HOAL line point the right way at Raasdorf? A value near 1 means the line has the right shape and only its level was off. A value near 0 or negative means the HOAL relationship does not hold at Raasdorf.


rows = []
for target in chosen:
    predicted = predictions[target].to_numpy()
    observed = raasdorf_2024[target].to_numpy()

    shifted_errors = []
    mean_errors = []
    for i in range(len(observed)):
        others = np.arange(len(observed)) != i
        shift = (observed[others] - predicted[others]).mean()
        shifted_errors.append(observed[i] - (predicted[i] + shift))
        mean_errors.append(observed[i] - observed[others].mean())

    same_points = observed - (predicted + (observed - predicted).mean())

    rows.append({
        "texture": target,
        "RMSE straight transfer": np.sqrt(np.mean((observed - predicted) ** 2)),
        "RMSE shifted, same points": np.sqrt(np.mean(same_points ** 2)),
        "RMSE shifted, leave-one-out": np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(shifted_errors))),
        "RMSE local mean, leave-one-out": np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(mean_errors))),
        "slope of observed on predicted": stats.linregress(predicted, observed).slope,
    })

recalibration = pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2)
recalibration

We decided in advance what counts as success. The recalibration is worth using only if:

the leave-one-out RMSE of the shifted line is below the local-mean RMSE, and
the slope of observed on predicted is close to 1.

If either fails, the shift is only hiding a relationship that does not hold at the new site.

title: A2: Recalibrating the intercept
text:
Step 4: the recalibrated equation
This is the equation you would report. It uses all 19 Raasdorf samples to set the shift. Its expected error is the leave-one-out number from step 3, not the “same points” number.

for target, predictor in chosen.items():
    fit = hoal_fits[target]
    shift = (raasdorf_2024[target] - predictions[target]).mean()
    print(f"{target}, HOAL line:      y = {fit.slope:.2f} x {predictor} {fit.intercept:+.1f}")
    print(f"{target}, recalibrated:   y = {fit.slope:.2f} x {predictor} {fit.intercept + shift:+.1f}   (shift {shift:+.1f})")

Clay, HOAL line:      y = -1.08 x U238 +78.7
Clay, recalibrated:   y = -1.08 x U238 +50.8   (shift -27.9)
Silt, HOAL line:      y = 1.08 x U238 +14.3
Silt, recalibrated:   y = 1.08 x U238 +20.0   (shift +5.6)

title: A2: Recalibrating the intercept
text:
Limits to keep in mind






Warning




It fixes the level, not the relationship. The slope stays the HOAL slope, so the line ranks samples exactly as before (janssen2008?). With few samples and a weak correlation, correcting the slope as well is not advisable, because it would be too uncertain (dardenne2004?).
It needs local lab data. The result is “the HOAL equation plus some Raasdorf samples”, not a pure transfer.
Only 19 samples. Every number above is rough.
The real test is still to come. When the Raasdorf_2026 lab results arrive, apply this recalibrated line to them without changing it. Those samples were not used to set the shift, so they are the fairest test of all.

title: Exploratory data analysis
text:
getting the data
summary statistics .describe() for each table, plus missing values, zeros and negatives in U238
Histograms: clay, silt and sand for HOAL vs Raasdorf_2024, and U238, K40 and Th232 for all three datasets.
Correlation: your heatmap and VIF (Step 2) belong here, not in the modelling.
Data checks: do sand and silt and clay add up to 100%? How far apart are the 19 Raasdorf points from their nearest survey reading (dist_m)? Are there duplicate coordinates?
The goal of this analysis is a transfer model: fit a relationship between gamma-ray values and soil texture at one site (HOAL), then use it at another (Raasdorf). A transfer only works if the two sites look alike. So the questions on this page are simple ones:

title: Exploratory data analysis
text:
Set up

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: Exploratory data analysis
text:
Getting data
This loads and renames the same three tables as Loading gamma-ray and soil data, in one go.

hoal = pd.read_csv("data/HOAL.csv")
hoal = hoal.rename(columns={"Sand_2023": "Sand", "Clay_2023": "Clay", "Silt_2023": "Silt"})

raasdorf_2024 = pd.read_csv("data/Raasdorf_2024.csv")

raasdorf_2026 = pd.read_csv("data/Raasdorf_2026.csv")
raasdorf_2026 = raasdorf_2026.rename(columns={"40-K": "K40", "238-U": "U238", "232-Th": "Th232"})

for table in (hoal, raasdorf_2024, raasdorf_2026):
    table["Ratio"] = table["U238"] / table["Th232"].replace(0, np.nan)

isotopes = ["K40", "U238", "Th232"]
texture = ["Clay", "Silt", "Sand"]

title: Exploratory data analysis
text:
Zeros in the Raasdorf_2026 survey
Some rows in the survey have an isotope value of exactly zero. These zeros are not measurements of “no uranium”. They come from the way the spectra are analysed.
The standard least-squares fit can return negative concentrations when a spectrum has very few counts, because the maths is happy with negative values. To avoid that, the survey is analysed with non-negative least squares (NNLS): if a concentration comes out negative, it is set to zero and the fit is repeated with the remaining nuclides (medusa_negative?). The constraint itself was introduced into full-spectrum analysis to avoid non-physical results (caciolli2011?).
A zero therefore means “too weak to say”, not “measured as zero”. We count them, keep a copy of the full survey for the map further down, and then drop every row where K40, U238 or Th232 is zero:

print(f"Rows in the survey: {len(raasdorf_2026)}")
for iso in isotopes:
    print(f"{iso}: {(raasdorf_2026[iso] == 0).sum()} zeros")

survey_all = raasdorf_2026.copy()
raasdorf_2026 = raasdorf_2026[(raasdorf_2026[isotopes] > 0).all(axis=1)]

print(f"Rows kept: {len(raasdorf_2026)}")
print(f"Rows dropped: {len(survey_all) - len(raasdorf_2026)}")

Rows in the survey: 2019
K40: 1 zeros
U238: 273 zeros
Th232: 68 zeros
Rows kept: 1678
Rows dropped: 341


The > 0 test also removes any negative or missing value, so it is safe even if the file changes later. We filter on the three natural isotopes only. Cs137 is also in the file, but the analysis doesn’t use it.
From here on we work with the cleaned tables. We put them in one dictionary so later code can loop over them:

tables = {"HOAL": hoal, "Raasdorf_2024": raasdorf_2024, "Raasdorf_2026": raasdorf_2026}







WarningWhat dropping the zeros costs



The dropped rows are, most often, spectra with very few counts. Removing them cuts off the low end of the distribution. The values that remain are, on average, a little higher than the full survey, and low-signal spots are under-represented. The Medusa documentation points to the same thing: because negatives are clamped to zero, the distribution of concentrations has a cut-off at zero and no longer follows Poisson statistics (medusa_negative?).
How large the effect is depends on how many rows are dropped. That is why we print the counts above and map where the dropped rows are, below. An alternative is to keep the zeros and treat them as “below detection”, but that is more complex, so we drop them and state the limitation.

title: Exploratory data analysis
text:
Histograms

Soil texture: HOAL vs Raasdorf_2024
The two sites have different numbers of samples, so the histograms show density instead of counts. That way the bars are comparable.

bins = np.arange(0, 101, 10)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
for ax, col in zip(axes, texture):
    ax.hist(hoal[col], bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="HOAL")
    ax.hist(raasdorf_2024[col], bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="Raasdorf_2024")
    ax.set_xlabel(f"{col} (%)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








With only a handful of samples per site, treat these shapes as a rough guide.


Gamma-ray values: all three datasets
The grey band marks the range of HOAL, where the model is fitted. Raasdorf values outside the band mean the model would have to extrapolate.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))

for ax, iso in zip(axes, isotopes):
    for name, table in tables.items():
        if name == "Raasdorf_2026":
            continue
        ax.hist(table[iso].dropna(), bins="auto", alpha=0.5, label=name)

    ax.set_xlabel(f"{iso} (Bq/kg)")

axes[0].set_ylabel("Count")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








The same thing in numbers: the share of Raasdorf values that fall outside the HOAL range.

rows = []
for iso in isotopes:
    hoal_vals = hoal[iso].dropna()
    low, high = hoal_vals.min(), hoal_vals.max()

    for name in ["Raasdorf_2024"]:
        values = tables[name][iso].dropna()
        outside = ((values < low) | (values > high)).mean() * 100
        rows.append({
            "isotope": iso,
            "HOAL range": f"{low:.1f} to {high:.1f}",
            "Raasdorf 2024 range": f"{values.min():.1f} to {values.max():.1f}",
            "% outside": round(outside, 1),
            "n": len(values),
        })

title: Exploratory data analysis
text:
Correlation
A correlation matrix shows, in one picture, which columns move together. We draw it for HOAL and for Raasdorf_2024 side by side, because a transfer model only makes sense if the isotopes relate to texture in the same direction at both sites.

def heatmap(ax, table, title):
    cols = texture + isotopes
    corr = table[cols].corr()

    image = ax.imshow(corr, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(cols)), cols, rotation=45, ha="right")
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(cols)), cols)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    ax.grid(False)

    for i, j in np.ndindex(corr.shape):
        value = corr.iloc[i, j]
        color = "white" if abs(value) > 0.5 else "black"
        ax.text(j, i, f"{value:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", color=color, fontsize=8)

    ax.set_title(title)
    return image

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    1, 3,
    figsize=(13, 5),
    gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 0.05, 1]},
)
heatmap(axes[0], hoal, f"HOAL (n={len(hoal)})")
image = heatmap(axes[2], raasdorf_2024, f"Raasdorf_2024 (n={len(raasdorf_2024)})")
fig.colorbar(image, cax=axes[1])
plt.show()








Two things to look for. First, whether the signs of the isotope-texture correlations (K40, U238 and Th232 against clay, silt and sand) match between the panels. Second, how strongly the three isotopes correlate with each other, because two predictors that track each other carry the same information twice.
HOAL (n = 13). Clay and silt are almost perfectly opposed (r = −0.99), so sand barely varies and the two carry the same signal. Both relate strongly to U238 (clay −0.89, silt +0.89), and clay also to Th232 (−0.71).
Raasdorf_2024 (n = 19). Clay and silt are only weakly opposed (r = −0.44), so sand varies independently. The isotope-texture correlations are weak: clay and U238 are +0.41, against −0.89 at HOAL, and sand and K40 are −0.52, against +0.17 at HOAL.
The relationships seen at HOAL do not appear at Raasdorf. A model fitted on HOAL should therefore not be expected to transfer without adjustment.

title: Exploratory data analysis
text:
Where the points are
The Raasdorf_2024 table has a position for each point. We check that no two points share the same coordinates:

duplicates = raasdorf_2024.duplicated(subset=["Longitude", "Latitude"]).sum()
print(f"Raasdorf_2024 points sharing exact coordinates with another point: {duplicates}")

Raasdorf_2024 points sharing exact coordinates with another point: 3


And we plot the 2026 survey, with the rows dropped for zeros in red, so you can see whether the dropped rows are scattered evenly or concentrated in one area. The Raasdorf_2024 points are shown as triangles.

dropped = survey_all.drop(raasdorf_2026.index)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
ax.scatter(raasdorf_2026["Longitude_GPS"], raasdorf_2026["Latitude_GPS"],
           s=6, color="gray", label="Survey, kept")
ax.scatter(dropped["Longitude_GPS"], dropped["Latitude_GPS"],
           s=6, color="crimson", label="Survey, dropped (zeros)")
ax.scatter(raasdorf_2024["Longitude"], raasdorf_2024["Latitude"],
           marker="^", s=40, color="black", label="Raasdorf_2024 points")
ax.set_aspect(1 / np.cos(np.radians(survey_all["Latitude_GPS"].mean())))
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude")
ax.set_ylabel("Latitude")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()

title: Exploratory data analysis
text:
Before moving on
The plots above should answer three questions: do the textures overlap, are the Raasdorf isotope values inside the HOAL range, and do the isotopes and texture move together in the same direction at both sites. If the answer to any of them is “not really”, that is a limit on what a transfer model can do, and we carry it into the modelling pages.

title: Getting set up
text: This guide gets your computer ready to run the Raasdorf soil texture notebook. You will install Python, an editor, and five packages. It takes about 15 minutes.

title: Getting set up
text:
Install Python
Download Python 3.10 or later from python.org and run the installer.






WarningWindows users



On the first screen of the installer, tick Add python.exe to PATH. If you forget, your terminal won’t find Python and the next steps will fail.


To check it worked, open a terminal and run:


Terminal

python --version

You should see something like Python 3.12.x. On macOS and Linux, the command may be python3 instead of python. If so, use python3 everywhere in this guide.






TipLinux (Debian / Ubuntu)



You also need the tool that creates virtual environments:


Terminal

sudo apt install python3-venv

title: Getting set up
text:
Install an editor
You need somewhere to open the notebook and run the code. Pick one. Both are free and both work well.

Option 1: Positron (recommended)
Download Positron and install it. It is built for data science: you see your code, your plots, and your variables all in one window, and it runs Python and R side by side.
Once it is installed, open it and check that it found Python: look at the interpreter picker in the bottom status bar. If you don’t see your Python version there, click the picker and choose it from the list.


Option 2: Visual Studio Code
If you already use VS Code, you can stay with it. Positron is built on the same foundation, so it will feel familiar. Install these two extensions from the Extensions panel:

Python (by Microsoft)
Jupyter (by Microsoft)

Without the Jupyter extension, VS Code can’t open .ipynb notebooks.

title: Getting set up
text:
Get the project files
Go to the project repository on GitHub, click Code -> Download ZIP, and unzip it.
If you already use git, you can clone it instead:


Terminal

git clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git

The folder contains the notebook (soil_texture_raasdorf.ipynb) and a file called requirements.txt. That file is the list of packages we use.

title: Getting set up
text:
Open the project folder
Open the whole project folder in your editor, not just the notebook file.

Positron or VS Code: File -> Open Folder…, then choose the project folder.

This matters because the next step creates the environment inside this folder, and the editor needs to be looking at the same place.

title: Getting set up
text:
Create your environment
Think of a virtual environment as a clean lab bench just for this project. The packages you install on it stay on it, so they never clash with other Python projects on your computer.
Open a terminal inside your editor (Terminal -> New Terminal). It opens in the project folder already.
Step 1. Create the environment. This makes a hidden folder called .venv:


Terminal

title: Gamma Ray Sensor
text:
The course

Getting set up: install R, Positron, and the packages this course uses.
The full pipeline: load, preprocess, tune, test, and predict, once, end to end, before any of it gets explained.
Loading spectral data: read a folder of OPUS files and a wet chemistry CSV into one tibble.
Exploratory data analysis: look at the spectra and the soil properties before modelling anything.
Feature engineering: build a recipes pipeline out of resampling, SNV, and Savitzky-Golay steps.
Outlier detection: use PCA on the preprocessed spectra to find samples a model shouldn’t trust.
Evaluating performance: split the data, fit a model, and score it with tidymodels.
Preparing a model for inference: save a fitted model, load it again, and predict new spectra.
Preparing OSSL: pull a working sample from the Open Soil Spectral Library.
Predicting exchangeable potassium using OSSL: the same pipeline, run end to end on a public, global dataset.

title: A: HOAL to Raasdorf_2024
text: This section asks one question: can a model built at HOAL predict soil texture at Raasdorf?

title: A: HOAL to Raasdorf_2024
text:
Site of the study






Figure 1: Site study and sampling points.



The plan has five steps:

Fit a straight line between each gamma-ray predictor and each texture class at HOAL.
Choose the best predictor, using HOAL only.
Check that the chosen line fits HOAL well enough to trust.
Check that the two sites overlap in texture.
Apply the line to the Raasdorf_2024 points, without changing anything, and compare the predictions with the lab values.

title: A: HOAL to Raasdorf_2024

Set up

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from scipy import stats

from pipeline import load_data, transfer
from plot_style import COLORS, LINE_COLOR, add_header

Sand has no relationship with any predictor (R² close to 0). It only ranges from about 6 to 8% at HOAL, so there is almost nothing to predict. We leave sand out from here on and transfer clay and silt.

title: A: HOAL to Raasdorf_2024
text:
Choose the predictor
We choose the predictor using HOAL only, before looking at any Raasdorf texture value. If we picked whichever predictor works best at Raasdorf, the test would no longer be independent. Two rules:

Low error at HOAL. We use leave-one-out RMSE. Each HOAL sample is left out in turn, the line is fitted on the other 12, and that line predicts the sample that was left out. The RMSE of those predictions is an honest estimate of the error on a new sample.
Raasdorf stays inside HOAL’s range. We count how many Raasdorf_2024 isotope values fall outside the range HOAL was measured on. This uses the isotope values only, not the texture. A model has to extrapolate outside that range.


def loo_rmse(x, y):
    errors = []
    for i in range(len(x)):
        train = np.arange(len(x)) != i
        fit = stats.linregress(x[train], y[train])
        errors.append(y[i] - (fit.intercept + fit.slope * x[i]))
    return np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(errors)))

rows = []
for target in targets:
    for predictor in predictors:
        x = hoal[predictor].to_numpy()
        y = hoal[target].to_numpy()
        values = raasdorf_2024[predictor]
        outside = ((values < x.min()) | (values > x.max())).mean() * 100
        rows.append({
            "target": target,
            "predictor": predictor,
            "LOO RMSE": loo_rmse(x, y),
            "% Raasdorf 2024 isotope outside HOAL range": outside,
        })

Check the chosen model
Before using the lines, we check how they miss. A residual is the observed value minus the fitted value. If the line is a good description, the residuals scatter around zero with no curve and no funnel shape.

for target in ["Clay", "Silt"]:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))
for ax, target in zip(axes, ["Clay", "Silt"]):

    residual = hoal[f"{target}_residual"]
    worst = residual.abs().nlargest(4).index

    ax.scatter(fitted[worst], residual[worst], s=65, color=COLORS[target],
               edgecolor="white", zorder=4)

        ax.annotate(hoal.loc[i, "Sample"], (fitted[i], residual[i]),
                    xytext=(6, 4), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8, color="#334155")

    ax.axhline(0, color=LINE_COLOR, linewidth=1.5)
    add_header(ax, f"{target} ~ U238: residuals (4 largest in colour)")

    ax.set_ylabel("Residual (%)")

plt.show()

Check that the two sites overlap in texture
The isotope check above is not enough. The textures must overlap too, or the model has to predict values it never saw.

title: A: HOAL to Raasdorf_2024
section: Apply the HOAL model to Raasdorf_2024
text:
Apply the HOAL model to Raasdorf_2024
Now the test. The line for each texture is fitted once on all the HOAL samples, then applied to the Raasdorf_2024 U238 values. Nothing is refitted on Raasdorf. We compare the predictions with the lab values using four numbers:

bias: the average of predicted minus observed. Zero means no systematic over- or under-prediction.
RMSE: the typical size of the error, in percentage points of texture.
baseline RMSE: the error we would get by always predicting the HOAL mean texture, with no model. A useful model has to beat it.
R2 transfer: how much better the model is than predicting the Raasdorf mean. It can be negative, which means the model does worse than that.


chosen = {"Clay": "U238", "Silt": "U238"}

rows = []
predictions = {}
for target, predictor in chosen.items():
    # Fit the line at HOAL, the reference site
    fit = stats.linregress(hoal[predictor], hoal[target])

    # Put the Raasdorf gamma-ray values into the HOAL line (nothing is refitted)
    predicted = fit.intercept + fit.slope * raasdorf_2024[predictor]
    predictions[target] = predicted

    # Compare with the lab values
    observed = raasdorf_2024[target]
    error = predicted - observed

    rows.append({
        "target": target,
        "predictor": predictor,
        "bias": error.mean(),
        "RMSE": np.sqrt((error ** 2).mean()),
        "baseline RMSE": np.sqrt(((hoal[target].mean() - observed) ** 2).mean()),
        "R2 transfer": 1 - (error ** 2).sum() / ((observed - observed.mean()) ** 2).sum(),
    })

We use U238 because it had the lowest error at HOAL and the best overlap with the new site’s values (see “Choose the predictor”). To try another site or predictor, only the tables and the chosen line change.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.5))
for ax, target in zip(axes, chosen):
    observed = raasdorf_2024[target]
    predicted = predictions[target]
    low = min(observed.min(), predicted.min()) - 2
    high = max(observed.max(), predicted.max()) + 2

    ax.plot([low, high], [low, high], color=LINE_COLOR, linewidth=1.5, linestyle="--", zorder=2)
    ax.scatter(observed, predicted, s=55, color=COLORS[target],

    ax.set_ylabel("Predicted from HOAL (%)")

    ax.set_ylim(low, high)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








The direct transfer does not work, because the two sites have different soils. Every Raasdorf_2024 clay value (4 to 12%) is below the lowest HOAL value (20%), and Raasdorf has about 29% sand where HOAL has about 7%. The model was therefore asked to predict textures it never saw. The isotope check did not catch this: U238 overlaps well, but the textures do not. A transfer needs the reference and target sites to overlap in texture as well as in gamma-ray values.

title: A: HOAL to Raasdorf_2024
text:
Limits to keep in mind






Warning




Only 13 HOAL samples. Every number above is rough.
A gap in the HOAL data. No HOAL sample has a U238 value between about 41 and 47 Bq/kg, and the two worst-fitted samples sit on either side of that gap. The line is untested there.
Only U238 could be used. Th232 is entirely outside the HOAL range at Raasdorf, and K40 and the ratio are about half outside.
Sand is not modelled, because it hardly varies at HOAL.
This is a test, not a proof. A good result here says the transfer worked for these 19 points, not that it will work everywhere.




rows = []
for target in ["Clay", "Silt"]:
    predicted = predictions[target].to_numpy()
    observed = raasdorf_2024[target].to_numpy()

    shifted_errors = []
    mean_errors = []
    for i in range(len(observed)):
        others = np.arange(len(observed)) != i
        shift = (observed[others] - predicted[others]).mean()
        shifted_errors.append(observed[i] - (predicted[i] + shift))
        mean_errors.append(observed[i] - observed[others].mean())

    rows.append({
        "texture": target,
        "slope of observed on predicted": stats.linregress(predicted, observed).slope,
        "LOO RMSE, HOAL line shifted": np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(shifted_errors))),
        "LOO RMSE, local mean only": np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(mean_errors))),
    })

pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2)

Re-calibration-of-the-large / intercept correction
Recalibration of the intercept, keeping the slope from the reference site, is a standard model-updating method (janssen2008?) and the simplest form of bias correction in calibration transfer (dardenne2004?). Because it leaves the slope unchanged, it corrects the level of the predictions but not how well they rank the samples.
